issues.legal_issue: A preventive authority may temporarily restrict otherwise lawful conduct, including conduct on a person's own property, when allowing it would be impracticable in the circumstances and it creates a danger to the public.
material_facts: The review applicants asked the Court to explain the principles governing preventive orders concerning property and public order.

The Court explained that an otherwise legal act on a person's own property may create danger to others or to public peace, and that excited feelings in an area may make it impracticable to permit the act.
issues.conclusion: A temporary preventive direction may restrict otherwise lawful conduct when that conduct creates the relevant public danger and it is impracticable to allow it in the circumstances; the authority must otherwise aid and protect persons acting lawfully.
issues.legal_principle: Section 144 authorizes directions to abstain from an act or to take certain action concerning property under a person's possession or management. Under Section 144(3), directions may address an individual or the public generally at a particular place; under Section 144(6), they are temporary and cannot last beyond two months. The directions are preventive, aimed at dangers to life, health, safety, peace or tranquillity, and must be assessed in light of the circumstances. No earlier case is relied on for this explanation.

predicates.preventive_order_proceeding: An authority is considering a temporary direction intended to prevent danger to the public.
predicates.public_danger_from_lawful_conduct: A person proposes conduct that is otherwise lawful, but that conduct creates danger to public life, health, safety, peace or tranquillity.
predicates.allowing_conduct_impracticable: The circumstances, including excited feelings in the area, make it impracticable to allow the conduct.

issues.definition: When a preventive-order proceeding concerns otherwise lawful conduct that creates public danger and cannot practicably be allowed, the conduct may be temporarily restricted.

issues.legal_issue: A dispute about title cannot be decided for the first time in a preventive-order proceeding or a writ proceeding, and a civil suit for an injunction is the remedy for resolving the dispute.
material_facts: The parties made conflicting assertions about rights to property connected with the preventive orders.
The review applicants asserted that an earlier representative suit had already decided title to the properties or places concerned.

The Court stated that title could not be decided for the first time in the proceedings before it and that a civil suit for an injunction was the remedy where one community or sect habitually transgressed another's property rights.
issues.conclusion: Title cannot be determined for the first time in a preventive-order or writ proceeding; a civil suit for an injunction is the appropriate remedy for resolving the title dispute or protecting the asserted property rights.
issues.legal_principle: Questions of title are not to be decided for the first time in a proceeding under Section 144 of the Criminal Procedure Code or in a writ proceeding under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. Where a community or sect habitually transgresses another's rights in property, the remedy lies in a civil suit for an injunction. No earlier case is relied on for this principle.

predicates.title_dispute_first_raised: A party asks the court or authority to resolve a title dispute that has not already been determined.
predicates.preventive_order_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding in which an authority is considering a temporary preventive direction.
predicates.writ_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding asking a court to exercise writ jurisdiction.

issues.definition: When an unresolved title dispute is raised in a preventive-order or writ proceeding, title is not decided in that proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A preventive authority may act only when public safety, peace, tranquillity or another purpose of the preventive power is in danger; without such danger, the parties must be directed to the proper forum.
material_facts: The Court explained that the authority's role was to respond to a public-order situation, not to determine individual rights.
The parties made conflicting assertions concerning property, and the Court stated that the authority could not act if public peace, tranquillity or other protected interests were not in danger.
issues.conclusion: If the relevant public interests are not in danger, the authority cannot issue a preventive direction and should direct the parties to the proper forum; if they are in danger, it may take appropriate action.
issues.legal_principle: Section 144 is a preventive power directed to dangers to life, health, safety, public peace or tranquillity, and the authority must decide what is reasonably necessary or expedient in the situation. It is not a means to adjudicate individual rights. No earlier case is relied on for this principle.

predicates.preventive_order_proceeding: An authority is considering a temporary direction intended to prevent danger to the public.
predicates.public_interest_in_danger: Public safety, peace, tranquillity or another protected public interest is in danger.

issues.definition: If an authority is considering a preventive direction and no protected public interest is in danger, it must not issue that direction.

issues.legal_issue: A prior judgment on title may inform the preventive authority's decision about whether, and what, preventive direction to issue, even though the authority cannot determine title itself.
material_facts: The review applicants asserted that an earlier representative suit had decided title to the properties or places connected with the preventive orders.
The Court stated that, if such a decision existed, the authority should respect it when deciding who should be allowed to exercise legitimate rights at the property.
issues.conclusion: A prior judgment on title may be considered and should be respected when the authority decides whether, and what, preventive direction is appropriate.
issues.legal_principle: Although title cannot be decided for the first time in a proceeding under Section 144, prior judgments concerning title may bear on whether, and what, order should be made. The authority must still decide what is reasonably necessary or expedient in the situation and is not adjudicating individual rights. No earlier case is cited for this principle.

predicates.preventive_order_proceeding: An authority is considering a temporary direction intended to prevent danger to the public.
predicates.prior_title_judgment_exists: A court has previously given judgment on title to property relevant to the preventive-order decision.

issues.definition: When a preventive-order proceeding concerns property for which a prior title judgment exists, the authority must consider that judgment.
